challenges.analysis: The source identifies the symbols as a Braille alphabet, so a Braille decoder is the direct first tool.

challenges.title: rev103
challenges.overview: rev103 is a Python-packed executable with a five-byte K0CTF seed used to generate an XOR stream.
challenges.analysis: DIE identifies the packer; extracting and decompiling rev103.pyc reveals the weak deterministic PRNG design.

steps.title: Identify the executable format

images.caption: The extractor recovers the Python bytecode.

steps.title: Decompile the bytecode
text: I decompiled rev103.pyc with PyLingual. The source showed a five-byte key used to seed Python random, then XORed every byte with predictable getrandbits(8) output.

images.alt: The recovered Python logic reveals the PRNG/XOR transformation.
images.caption: The recovered Python logic reveals the PRNG/XOR transformation.

steps.title: Reproduce the transformation
text: I saved the recovered transformation as a script. It uses the first five bytes as the little-endian seed and XORs the same pseudorandom stream, matching the documented code path.

challenges.result: The predictable PRNG stream recovered the flag.
challenges.learned: Packing is not encryption. Once recovered bytecode reveals a short predictable seed, the stream can be reproduced exactly.

challenges.title: rev105
challenges.overview: The source calls this challenge Rev105; it is mapped to the requested rec105 title. The binary is UPX-packed and validates consecutive character pairs using sums, truncated products, and XORs.
challenges.analysis: DIE identifies UPX, and Ghidra exposes the three validation arrays after unpacking. The multiplication check uses only the low byte.

steps.title: Check packing with DIE
text: I first analysed rev105 with DIE. It showed that the binary was UPX-packed, so static analysis needed an unpacked copy.

images.alt: The rev105 challenge prompt.
images.caption: The rev105 challenge prompt.

images.alt: DIE identifies the UPX packing.
images.caption: DIE identifies the UPX packing.

steps.title: Unpack the executable
text: I unpacked the file with UPX and checked it again before loading it in Ghidra.

images.alt: The unpacked executable is ready for analysis.
images.caption: The unpacked executable is ready for analysis.

steps.title: Read the three validation arrays
text: Ghidra showed a triple validation system over consecutive character pairs. I recorded the sum, byte-truncated product, and XOR arrays from the DAT locations.

images.alt: Ghidra exposes the validation arrays.
images.caption: Ghidra exposes the validation arrays.

steps.title: Solve each adjacent pair
text: For every position, I searched for characters a and b satisfying a + b = sum, (a * b) & 0xFF = product, and a ^ b = xor. Chaining the solutions reconstructs the 32-character flag.

steps.title: Run the documented pair solver
text: The original write-up states the three equations but does not preserve its own script. I added a reusable, source-faithful solver that accepts the sum, low-byte-product, and XOR arrays copied from Ghidra.

It searches printable character pairs, chains neighbouring pairs, and checks the wrap-around condition described in the write-up. This makes the stated method reproducible without pretending that the missing original script was recovered.

challenges.result: The chained pairwise constraints recovered the flag.
challenges.learned: Model byte truncation exactly when reversing native validation logic.

challenges.title: Call_me
challenges.overview: The binary reads 200 bytes into an 80-byte buffer and calls a function pointer 72 bytes from the buffer start. The flag function is yo_chat_is_this_real at 0x40123b.
challenges.analysis: The source describes no PIE, no canary, a known offset, and a target function, which forms a direct function-pointer overwrite.

steps.title: Inspect the binary properties
text: The challenge binary’s vuln function reads 200 bytes into an 80-byte buffer. The source notes no PIE, no stack canaries, and an executable stack, so a function-pointer overwrite is viable.

images.alt: The Call_me challenge and downloadable binary.
images.caption: The Call_me challenge and downloadable binary.

steps.title: Calculate the overwrite offset
text: The buffer begins at rbp-0x50 and the function pointer is at rbp-0x8. The difference is 72 bytes, so the payload needs 72 bytes of padding before the replacement address.

steps.title: Choose the flag function
text: The source identifies yo_chat_is_this_real at 0x40123b as the only useful target. The documented payload structure is therefore 72 padding bytes followed by that address in the target’s byte order.

steps.title: Run the payload and read the output
text: Executing the exploit redirected the function pointer to the flag-printing function.

images.alt: The exploit result prints the Call_me flag.
images.caption: The exploit result prints the Call_me flag.

challenges.result: The 72-byte function-pointer overwrite returned the flag.
challenges.learned: A memory-corruption exploit should be derived from the exact buffer-to-pointer offset and the intended control-flow target.
